label: Homology
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 339 through 380 and builds the singular homology functor. The recurring question is which cycles fail to be boundaries, since exactly those failures detect holes. We replace loops and surfaces by signed chains so topology becomes computable abelian algebra.

label: Singular Simplices and Chains
notes: A singular p-simplex is any continuous map from the standard simplex, allowed to fold or collapse. Free integer combinations of these maps form the chain group C_p. The geometry need not embed cleanly; the algebra only needs ordered vertices so each face carries a definite sign.

label: The Boundary Operator
notes: The boundary operator takes the alternating sum of a simplex restricted to its faces, dropping one vertex at a time. The triangle here shows oriented edges whose signed sum cancels at shared vertices. This single alternating-sign rule drives every later cancellation argument in the chapter.

label: Boundary of a Boundary is Zero
notes: Applying the boundary twice gives zero because every codimension-two face appears exactly twice with opposite signs. This identity makes image of one boundary sit inside the kernel of the next, which is the algebraic permission to form the homology quotient. The matrix product is exactly zero.

label: Cycles, Boundaries, Homology
notes: Cycles are chains with zero boundary; boundaries are chains produced by a higher chain. Since boundaries lie inside cycles, the quotient kernel modulo image is well defined. The n-th homology group records cycles that survive after every higher-dimensional filling has been subtracted away as trivial.

label: Functoriality
notes: A continuous map sends each singular simplex to its composite, and composing commutes with face restriction. So the induced chain map carries cycles to cycles and boundaries to boundaries, descending to homology. Homeomorphisms thus yield inverse isomorphisms, which is precisely why homology is a topological invariant.

label: Homotopy Invariance
notes: Homotopic maps induce equal homology maps. The proof triangulates the prism swept out by a homotopy; its side faces are exactly the correction term in the chain-homotopy identity. On a cycle the side correction vanishes, so the two images differ only by a boundary and agree in homology.

label: H0 Counts Components
notes: Zero-dimensional homology is free abelian on the path components of the space. Every point is a cycle, and a path between two points is a one-chain whose boundary identifies them. Thus H_0 has rank equal to the number of path components, the first concrete homology computation.

label: Homology of Spheres
notes: The n-sphere has homology Z in degrees zero and n and zero otherwise. This sharp result distinguishes spheres of different dimensions, proves invariance of dimension, and yields Brouwer fixed point and the hairy ball theorem. It is the benchmark every computational technique in the chapter must reproduce.

label: Mayer-Vietoris
notes: Mayer-Vietoris glues two open pieces into a long exact sequence linking their homology, the overlap, and the union. On the circle the overlap of two arcs has two components; their difference lies in a kernel that the connecting map fills, creating the one-dimensional loop class out of local data.

label: Hurewicz: H1 and pi1
notes: For a path-connected space, first homology is the abelianization of the fundamental group. Homology forgets the noncommutative order in which loops are traversed but gains an abelian group that linear algebra can compute. This is the precise bridge between Chapter twelve's pi_1 and the homology of this chapter.

label: Euler Characteristic
notes: The Euler characteristic is the alternating sum of cell counts and equally the alternating sum of Betti numbers. Boundary maps shuffle rank between adjacent degrees, but exact cancellation keeps the alternating total invariant. Torsion has rank zero, so it never contributes, which is why surfaces are classified by this single integer.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: Homology begins with the boundary-of-a-boundary identity and ends with a computable functor: H_0 counts components, H_1 abelianizes pi_1, spheres give Z in their own degree, Mayer-Vietoris assembles global classes, and the Euler characteristic survives as an alternating Betti sum. Cohomology will later reverse every arrow.
